plot_extraction.response_text:
As winter begins, cowboys Baugh, Stubb, and Arab Ab are laid off under new cattle-company rules that also deny unemployed range riders the customary food and shelter at ranch camps. They travel to a Kansas county seat intending to enjoy themselves until spring, but gambling and horse racing soon consume nearly all their money.

To survive the rest of the winter, Baugh devises a confidence scheme targeting Louie Seigerman, a German hotel-and-bar owner eager to hold public office. The three cowboys pose as influential representatives of major cattle companies and persuade him that cattlemen, angered by rampant theft, unanimously want him to run for sheriff. They promise vast political support, campaign funds, hundreds of imported votes, and even the prospect of eventually becoming a U.S. marshal.

Flattered and convinced, Seigerman declares his candidacy. Believing the cowboys to be his campaign managers, he provides them with free lodging, meals, liquor, and travel money for several months. When spring returns and ranch work is again available, the trio invents reports of political trouble, obtains final expense money, and disappears, leaving a letter claiming that urgent cattle business has called each of them away while assuring Seigerman of victory.

At the county convention, Seigerman receives only one vote on each ballot. The cowboys turn his humiliating result into the range expression “Seigerman’s Per Cent,” meaning the smallest or worst possible return.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a genial, anecdotal Western style, combining frontier realism with the shape and timing of a tall tale. Its third-person narrator is broadly omniscient but stays close to the outlook of the cattle range, explaining customs such as “chuck-line riding” and treating cowboy values as the natural frame of reference. The narrative voice is confident, sociable, and mildly ironic. It rarely condemns the central trio outright; instead, their fraud is presented as roguish ingenuity, while the impersonal cattle companies, political ambition, and local credulity form the wider objects of satire.

The diction mixes plain standard narration with period-specific range vocabulary: “pay-roll,” “brand,” “round-up,” “rustling,” “branding-chute,” and “sinews of war.” Biblical, political, military, and commercial phrases are humorously transplanted into cowboy life, as in “cast bread upon the waters,” “central committee,” and Baugh’s “tuition account.” This produces a comic contrast between the men’s precarious circumstances and the grand language with which they describe themselves. The prose also preserves archaic forms and spellings such as “towards,” “cheque,” “some one,” and “to-day,” giving it a late nineteenth- or early twentieth-century texture.

Dialogue dominates much of the story and carries both characterization and plot. Baugh speaks in expansive, theatrical boasts and strategic instructions; Stubb adopts a drier, skeptical manner; Arab amplifies every lie through extravagant statistics and practical claims about delivering votes. Their banter is affectionate but abrasive, filled with mock insults, oaths, gambling idioms, and comic undercutting. Repetition helps establish the trio’s rhythm: Baugh invents the scheme, Stubb lends it respectability, and Arab inflates it beyond plausibility. Seigerman’s speech is rendered through heavy phonetic German-accent spelling—“Dot ish my name” and “I accep”—a period caricatural convention that sharply distinguishes his voice but also makes ethnicity part of the joke.

Sentence structure varies according to function. Expository passages use measured, medium-to-long sentences to explain range life and economic conditions, while comic scenes proceed through brisk exchanges. The fraudulent campaign speeches are deliberately long, cumulative, and overloaded with plausible detail. Lists of cattle losses, political connections, company names, vote totals, and promised funds mimic the rhetoric of business and electioneering, allowing fabrication to acquire authority through specificity. Parenthetical comments and qualifying phrases add an oral, reminiscing quality, as though the narrator were retelling a well-known camp story.

The pacing is episodic and linear. It begins with social and economic background, narrows to the trio’s dismissal, follows their gambling losses, and then devotes the largest section to the escalating confidence trick. Repeated visits to Seigerman’s back room create a patterned comic progression: each man performs a role, the supposed political coalition grows, and Seigerman becomes steadily more committed. Several months are then compressed into a brief summary before the trio withdraws as spring returns. This seasonal structure is important: winter creates their need, the bogus campaign sustains them, and new grass releases them back into legitimate range work.

Humour arises chiefly from dramatic irony, exaggeration, incongruity, and delayed payoff. The reader understands that the political movement is fictitious while Seigerman interprets every refusal of drink, private conference, and invented credential as proof of professionalism. The trio’s temporary temperance is especially comic because it is purely tactical. Their increasingly grand coalition is marked through the mock-diplomatic sequence “Zweibund,” “Dreibund,” and “Fierbund,” elevating a bar-room swindle into an international alliance. The final revelation—that Seigerman receives one vote—provides a concise punch line, followed by a folkloric coda in which “Seigerman’s Per Cent” becomes range slang for the worst possible return.

Characterization is economical and behavioral rather than introspective. Baugh is defined by confidence, verbal control, physical presence, and improvisational intelligence. Stubb is the “conservative” whose apparent caution makes the deception credible, while Arab is the campaign “heeler,” expert in boasting about mass organization and electoral manipulation. Seigerman is characterized through hospitality, vanity, credulity, and political ambition. The narrator occasionally labels or summarizes these traits, but the men are chiefly revealed by how they talk, gamble, scheme, and respond to one another.

The underlying tone is amused rather than moralizing. The deception is ethically dubious, yet the story frames it as a survival strategy prompted by corporate stinginess and winter unemployment. Hospitality is treated as a central frontier virtue: the cattle companies’ withdrawal of food and shelter violates range custom, whereas Seigerman’s generosity—though exploited—keeps the men alive. At the same time, the tale satirizes electoral corruption, manufactured public opinion, inflated commercial authority, and the ease with which personal ambition can be manipulated. Overall, the style is colloquial, masculine, dialogue-heavy, regionally grounded, and structurally oriented toward a memorable comic ending, with realism supplying the setting and tall-tale exaggeration supplying the energy.

generation.response_text:
# Seigerman’s Per Cent

The winter which turned Baugh, Stubb, and Arab Ab loose upon the peace and finances of Comanche County began with a blue norther that froze three water barrels before supper and drove every loose yearling on the Cimarron ten miles south before daylight.

Up to that season an unemployed cow-hand had never been considered exactly destitute. He might be without wages, but so long as he could throw a leg over a horse he belonged, in a loose and wandering fashion, to the range. Any ranch whose brand he had ever worked could be depended upon for a meal, a bed in the bunk-house, and feed for his mount. If he met the outfit on the trail, the cook would set out a plate without asking for his pedigree or financial standing.

That was called riding the chuck-line. No one had invented it by statute, and therefore every one respected it.

But the cattle business had lately taken to wearing a white collar. Eastern money had come in, followed by bookkeepers, printed regulations, and gentlemen who could reckon the cost of a biscuit at forty rods. The old cattlemen had given a rider shelter because he might be useful at the next round-up. The new companies maintained that a man not on the pay-roll had no more claim upon beef and beans than a coyote had upon the branding-chute.

A circular came down from the head office of the Continental and Western Cattle Company declaring that, after the first of November, no food, lodging, horse feed, tobacco, medicine, ammunition, or other company supplies were to be furnished to persons not in regular employment.

The ranch superintendent read the order aloud in the cook-shack. When he finished, no one spoke for several seconds.

Then Arab Ab, who had been christened Abner and had earned the rest of his name by trading horses with a Syrian peddler, said:

“I notice they don’t prohibit us from breathing company air.”

“That’ll be in the next circular,” said Stubb.

Baugh took the paper from the superintendent and examined it gravely. He was a large, deliberate man whose confidence commonly arrived at a destination several minutes before the truth started. He read the regulation twice, turned it over to see if there were any mercy printed on the back, and handed it away.

“The cattle business,” he observed, “is advancing towards civilization. The first evidence of civilization is when hospitality gets entered on the wrong side of the ledger.”

The superintendent had no pleasure in discharging them. He needed fifty riders in the spring, but only twelve during the winter. The company had ordered him to cut the pay-roll, and a company order was a kind of weather: a man might criticize it, but he still got wet.

Thus Baugh, Stubb, and Arab Ab received their wages, rolled their beds, and started north.

They had between them seven horses, three saddles, two pack outfits, and a little more than four hundred dollars. This seemed enough to carry them until spring, especially to men accustomed to measuring wealth by whether it could be folded and put into a vest pocket. They intended to winter modestly in Willet, the county seat, and return to the range when the grass came.

Their modesty survived until the second evening.

Willet contained a court-house, a bank, two churches, four livery stables, a newspaper, and eleven places where a man could obtain evidence against himself. It also possessed Louie Seigerman’s hotel and bar, which stood opposite the court-house and enjoyed the trade of lawyers, jurors, drovers, traveling salesmen, and candidates for office.

Baugh and his companions secured a room there, ate a supper that reminded them they had not lately been fed by a corporation, and entered the bar to make the acquaintance of the county.

A poker game was in progress behind the stove.

“We will sit in for an hour,” said Baugh. “It is bad manners to enter a town and refuse its hospitality.”

At midnight Stubb had lost thirty-eight dollars.

At two o’clock Arab Ab remarked that he had discovered the habits of the game.

At three, after losing sixty more, he said that the habits of the game had changed without notice.

Baugh played until breakfast, explaining at intervals that temporary losses were merely tuition. When the game ended, his tuition account stood at one hundred and nine dollars.

Their next misfortune was a horse race. Arab owned a brown gelding which could outrun any horse he had ever raced against under fair conditions. Willet produced a gray mare that beat him by half a length under conditions which Arab described for three days and never once called fair.

Stubb then backed a bay horse belonging to a deputy assessor. The bay lost by forty yards and was afterwards discovered to have been entered chiefly on account of the deputy assessor’s need for money.

Baugh declined to be discouraged.

“Luck,” he said, “is a nervous animal. Chase it and it runs. Turn your back, and it’ll follow you home.”

They turned their backs on luck in a faro game and lost another eighty dollars.

By the middle of December they had sold two spare horses. By Christmas the pack animals had gone. They celebrated the holiday with a turkey dinner at Seigerman’s, after which Louie presented a bill that proved hospitality had entered politics as well as bookkeeping.

January found them with three saddle horses, their equipment, and twenty-seven dollars and forty cents.

The weather had hardened. Snow lay in the draws, the north wind swept the streets, and the range camps were closed to chuck-line riders. There was no work nearer than the Indian Territory, and perhaps none there. A cowboy will endure heat, thirst, dust, danger, and the society of a cook, but he does not willingly sell his saddle. The three therefore gathered in their room at Seigerman’s to consider measures of finance.

Stubb emptied their joint treasury onto the bed.

“Seven dollars and forty cents belongs to me,” he said. “Arab’s got nine. You possess eleven dollars and all the wisdom.”

“Wisdom,” said Baugh, “has been bringing a low market lately.”

Arab lay on the other bed with his boots against the wall.

“We can make a race with the black horse,” he suggested.

“We can also burn the money for warmth,” said Stubb. “It takes less time.”

“The black horse can run.”

“So can a barber, if you shoot close enough. That don’t make him a race horse.”

Baugh had been looking through the frost-furred window at the court-house. Several men stood on its steps, and one was shaking hands with every person who passed.

“Who is that energetic citizen?” he asked.

“Jim Tolliver,” Stubb answered. “Candidate for sheriff.”

“How many candidates are there?”

“Three declared. Tolliver, Mason, and old Ricks.”

“Then there is a vacancy.”

“There’s three men after one office.”

“That leaves a vacancy for a fourth man.”

Arab sat up. “You fixing to run?”

“I never accept an office unless it comes looking for me with a rope. But a public movement, properly encouraged, has its advantages.”

Stubb regarded him. “The last public movement you encouraged was a shell game at Dodge.”

“That was private enterprise. I am now considering the voice of the people.”

“The people ain’t said anything.”

“That’s why they require a spokesman.”

Baugh went downstairs. Seigerman was behind the bar polishing glasses. He was a round, prosperous man with pale whiskers, a broad red face, and a deep conviction that public office was the natural crown of success. He had once been elected precinct committeeman for the Reform Party, but the party had expired before he could take advantage of it. Since then he had served on school committees, welcomed conventions, contributed beer to torchlight parades, and mentioned to every traveling politician that he was ready to sacrifice himself for the county.

Baugh ordered three drinks and paid for them from the eleven dollars. This expenditure pained Stubb when he heard of it, but Baugh explained that capital must be cast upon the waters.

“Mr. Seigerman,” Baugh said, “you know the cattle interests.”

“I know many cattlemen,” said Louie. “They stop by my house. Good men. Sometimes they pay.”

“What is their feeling concerning law enforcement?”

Seigerman set down the glass he was polishing.

“They do not like thieves.”

“Precisely. Rustling has become the leading industry. A stockman brands a calf on Monday and meets it Wednesday wearing another man’s name. The cattle companies are aroused.”

“Dot sheriff, he does nothing?”

“I would not say nothing. A man standing still occupies space. But the companies want action. They want a fearless, impartial, substantial citizen—some one not controlled by the court-house ring.”

Seigerman’s towel moved more slowly.

“Who do they want?”

Baugh looked towards the door, then lowered his voice.

“I am not authorized to give names.”

“Sure. Sure. I understand.”

“I will say this: when representatives of seven of the largest brands in the Southwest met privately last month, one name was favorably discussed.”

Louie leaned across the bar.

“Whose name?”

Baugh glanced again at the door.

“The conference was confidential.”

“I am confidential.”

“That may be, but I have my instructions.”

He drank slowly, declined a second glass, and walked out.

The refusal of liquor impressed Seigerman more than anything he had said. Baugh had never before declined a drink in the house. A man who refused one at eleven in the morning must be carrying business of consequence.

When Baugh returned upstairs, Stubb demanded an accounting.

“You spent thirty cents to say what?”

“Nothing definite.”

“That’s the best thirty cents’ worth of your conversation I ever heard.”

“I have laid the foundation.”

“What are we building?”

“A sheriff.”

“Out of what?”

Baugh took off his hat and threw it on the bed.

“Out of Louie Seigerman’s ambition, which is the most plentiful building material in this county.”

Arab’s face brightened. “Is he going to run?”

“He is going to be summoned by the united cattle interests. We are the united cattle interests.”

Stubb pushed the coins together.

“What interest have they united on?”

“Keeping us alive until spring.”

For the next two days Baugh said no more to Seigerman. He paid for one meal, skipped another, and remained sober with a severity which disturbed his companions. On the third evening, while the bar was crowded, he entered, looked around as if seeking privacy, and said:

“Louie, have you a room where four men can confer without interruption?”

Seigerman led him at once to a small room behind the bar. There was a table, six chairs, a spittoon, and a framed photograph of the governor.

Baugh closed the door.

“The situation has developed,” he said. “I have received authority to proceed one step further. Before I do, I must know your attitude on rustling.”

“My attitude? I put them all in jail.”

“Good. Would you enforce the law against a small thief as well as a large one?”

“Sure.”

“Against a cowboy as well as a farmer?”

“Sure.”

“Against a company employee?”

“Every one.”

Baugh frowned. “The companies may not like that last answer.”

“I enforce dot law.”

He continued frowning for ten seconds. “It is the right answer. They may not like it, but they will respect it.”

Seigerman’s chest expanded.

“Now,” Baugh continued, “I am connected with the Continental and Western. You may know that.”

Louie did not, but nodded.

“I have been instructed to feel you out. No commitment. No promises. Merely determine whether, if a public demand arose, you would permit your name to be considered for sheriff.”

Seigerman’s face reddened beyond its customary color.

“For sheriff?”

“Do not misunderstand me. There are difficulties. The brands are divided over methods. The Bar-Circle wants a range man. The Diamond Tail opposes every one proposed by the Continental. The Boxed K has money but no organization. Yet all agree that the present candidates are too weak.”

“Do they say my name?”

Baugh looked pained.

“I cannot disclose the proceedings of a confidential conference.”

“But they say it?”

“I can tell you only that your record as a property owner, taxpayer, hotel man, former precinct committeeman, and friend of the livestock interest has not escaped attention.”

Seigerman breathed deeply.

“If dot people call me—if duty says, ‘Louie, you must go’—I do not run away.”

“That is all I am authorized to learn.”

“What happens now?”

“I consult the conservative element.”

“Who is dot?”

“Stubb.”

Seigerman had seen Stubb eating and drinking in the house, but had never detected any conservative element in him. This made the discovery more impressive.

An hour later Stubb was dragged from his room, informed of his dignity, and coached.

“You represent the Bar-Circle, the Diamond Tail, and the independent stockmen north of the river,” Baugh said. “You are opposed to Seigerman.”

“Why?”

“Because opposition is respectable. If we all fall on his neck at once, he may mistrust us. You raise objections. I answer them. Arab furnishes figures.”

“What figures?”

“Any he can lift.”

Arab nodded. “I can furnish figures enough to make the census look like a private memorandum.”

The conference took place the following afternoon. Stubb entered the back room reluctantly, carrying a folded newspaper and wearing the expression of a man summoned to identify a body. Baugh introduced him as a representative of several concerns whose combined herds, according to Arab’s later calculation, would have required most of Kansas for standing room.

Seigerman produced whisky and glasses.

“No,” said Baugh. “Not during business.”

Stubb looked at him with sincere resentment, which Louie mistook for official austerity.

“We may take one,” Stubb said.

“We may not,” Baugh replied. “The eyes of the cattle interests are upon us.”

“Their eyes ain’t thirsty.”

Baugh ignored him.

“Mr. Stubb has doubts concerning your availability, Louie. I considered it fair that you hear them directly.”

Stubb settled into his chair.

“I don’t favor a hotel man,” he said.

“Why not?” Seigerman demanded.

“Too many friends. A sheriff needs enemies.”

“I got enemies.”

“How many?”

“Plenty.”

“Can you name twelve reliable ones?”

Seigerman began counting. He reached eight without difficulty, hesitated, and remembered four men who had disputed bills.

“That’s better,” said Stubb. “Still, you’re foreign-born.”

“I am a citizen twenty-two years.”

“Some folks object to a man born outside the county.”

“I was born outside, but I live here longer than Tolliver.”

“True. Then there’s the liquor issue. The temperance people won’t support a saloonkeeper.”

“My hotel has food, rooms, stable—everything. The bar is only part.”

“The bar is the part they’ll mention.”

Baugh struck the table with his palm.

“Now we reach the heart of the matter. Are the cattlemen to let a handful of water-drinkers select their sheriff? The Continental loses twelve thousand dollars a year through theft. The Boxed K lost eight hundred and forty steers last season. The Diamond Tail estimates that one calf in six disappears before branding. Yet Stubb would reject the one man capable of stopping it because he sells an honest drink.”

“I didn’t say reject,” Stubb answered. “I said investigate.”

“The investigation has been proceeding for months.”

Seigerman looked from one to the other.

“Do they all want me?”

“No,” said Stubb.

“Yes,” said Baugh, at the same instant.

The disagreement pleased Louie. It proved that the meeting was genuine.

Stubb opened his newspaper.

“The Bar-Circle wants Peters.”

“Peters cannot carry the towns.”

“The Diamond Tail likes Hendry.”

“Hendry cannot carry his own household. His wife votes against him at breakfast.”

“The independents want a cowman.”

“They cannot agree upon which cowman. If one brand names a candidate, every neighboring brand recalls a quarrel over water.”

Stubb rubbed his chin.

“What about campaign funds?”

“The sinews of war will be supplied.”

“How much?”

Baugh looked at Seigerman. “That depends upon the candidate.”

Stubb shook his head. “You see? No organization. No figures. Just wind blowing across a big pasture.”

At this signal the door opened and Arab Ab entered without knocking. He wore a long coat borrowed from a horse dealer and carried a leather memorandum book.

“Am I interrupting the central committee?” he asked.

“You are,” said Baugh. “Come in.”

Arab bowed gravely to Seigerman.

“This is Mr. Ab,” said Baugh, “our organization man.”

“Organizer for who?” Stubb asked.

“For the voters,” said Arab. “Companies come and go, but voters remain unless the sheriff gets active.”

He opened his book.

“I have completed a preliminary canvas. The Continental can deliver one hundred and forty-two men. Bar-Circle, sixty-eight. Diamond Tail, ninety-one. Boxed K, one hundred and seventeen. Double Spur, forty-three. Independent riders and floaters, conservatively, two hundred and six.”

Stubb stared at him. “That’s six hundred and sixty-seven.”

Arab turned a page. “You omitted cooks.”

“How many cooks vote?”

“Every cook who can get away from his outfit, and some who can’t. Add thirty-four. Blacksmiths, twenty-one. Hide buyers, eleven. Livery employees, sixteen. Men unjustly accused of stealing horses, nine.”

“Why would they support a sheriff?”

“They favor a change of administration.”

Seigerman leaned over the book, but Arab closed it.

“Confidential rolls,” he explained.

“How many total?” Louie asked.

“Our first-line strength is seven hundred and fifty-eight. With proper inducements and transportation, we can bring in four hundred votes from adjoining counties.”

Stubb sat upright. “They can’t vote here.”

Arab looked offended.

“Not until they establish residence. We are discussing organization, not miracles.”

“How long does that take?”

“In politics, residence is chiefly a condition of mind.”

Baugh intervened.

“We will have no irregularities. Mr. Seigerman must be elected cleanly.”

“Certainly,” said Arab. “Clean as a washed cheque.”

The first conference ended without a decision. Stubb remained officially doubtful, Arab was ordered to verify his totals, and Baugh promised to communicate with the principal companies. Seigerman furnished supper to all three and refused payment.

“You are working for me,” he said.

“Not yet,” Baugh corrected. “We are working for the cattle interests.”

“Sure. Sure. I understand.”

The next morning their room bill was returned marked “By arrangement.”

Stubb examined it.

“I begin to respect public service,” he said.

“Do not cheapen the movement by enjoying it too soon,” Baugh warned. “Louie has been approached, but not nominated. We must enlarge the demand.”

“How large?”

“Large enough to include board, lodging, and horse feed until April.”

Arab suggested they send telegrams to themselves. Baugh rejected the idea as extravagant, but approved letters. During the next week they wrote communications upon paper bearing the names of cattle companies. The stationery was obtained by Arab from old invoices in a commission merchant’s office, and the messages were posted from three neighboring towns by obliging stage drivers.

Baugh received the first letter at breakfast. He read it, frowned, and put it into his pocket.

Seigerman came from behind the desk.

“News?”

“Nothing final.”

“From a company?”

“The Prairie Consolidated.”

“What do they say?”

“They are cautious.”

That afternoon Stubb received a letter from the Diamond Tail and allowed it to remain unopened on the bar for twenty minutes. The envelope attracted nearly as much attention as a weapon.

At supper Arab burst into the dining-room waving a third letter.

“Victory!” he cried, then checked himself upon seeing Seigerman. “I beg pardon. This is private.”

Louie took them all into the back room.

The Prairie Consolidated, as interpreted by Baugh, would support Seigerman if the northern interests did so. The Diamond Tail demanded assurance that he would appoint a range man as deputy. The Boxed K promised money after the convention. The Double Spur was unwilling to make promises but viewed the movement with “profound sympathy,” a phrase Baugh said was equivalent to forty votes.

“This makes the Zweibund,” he announced.

“What is dot?” Louie asked.

“A two-power alliance. The Continental and Prairie Consolidated.”

Stubb studied the governor’s portrait.

“You still need the Diamond Tail.”

“I have them conditionally.”

“Conditional cattle don’t make unconditional beef.”

Seigerman offered to promise a range deputy.

“Not yet,” said Baugh. “A candidate who begins promising offices before nomination loses moral force. Besides, Stubb may want the place.”

“I don’t,” said Stubb.

“Your reluctance qualifies you.”

Three days later the Diamond Tail was admitted, creating what Arab called the Dreibund. When the Boxed K entered, he declared a Fierbund, which Seigerman repeated proudly to customers although he could not explain its geography.

The campaign began to supply all necessities. Louie provided the three men a larger room, saying political leaders required space. Their horses were moved into his stable without charge. Meals appeared at any hour, and the back room was reserved for the central committee. A bottle stood on the table, but Baugh enforced temperance during conferences.

This discipline nearly ruined the scheme.

“I can lie without whisky,” Stubb complained, “but I don’t see why a man should be asked to.”

“A single drink might loosen confidential information.”

“There ain’t any information.”

“Then it is all the easier to keep confidential.”

Arab proved less obedient. He hid a glass behind the governor’s photograph until Baugh discovered it.

“You are endangering the confidence of the candidate.”

“I’m maintaining the enthusiasm of the voters.”

When Seigerman entered, Arab immediately opened his book and reported that the organization had grown to nine hundred and twelve men, not including sheepmen.

“I thought cattlemen hated sheep,” Louie said.

“They do. That makes sheepmen easy to organize against any candidate the cattlemen oppose.”

“But the cattlemen support me.”

“Exactly. The sheepmen will support you to show independence.”

Seigerman considered the reasoning and found it profound.

The formal call came late in January. Baugh had delayed it until Louie’s appetite for office had overcome his remaining caution. The three representatives assembled after midnight, when the bar was closed. They wore clean shirts, and Arab had persuaded the local printer to prepare a document headed:

**DECLARATION OF THE UNITED LIVESTOCK, COMMERCIAL, AGRICULTURAL, AND LAW-ABIDING INTERESTS OF COMANCHE COUNTY.**

The declaration stated that theft stalked unchecked, property trembled, justice slumbered, and the eyes of honest citizenship had turned spontaneously towards Louis Seigerman.

Baugh read it aloud.

“Mr. Seigerman,” he concluded, “we are instructed to ask whether you will accept the nomination for sheriff, subject to the action of the county convention and the sovereign people.”

Louie stood. His hands shook slightly, and for once his pleasure made him solemn.

“Gentlemen, I do not seek dot office. Many times people say, ‘Louie, you should be sheriff,’ and I say, ‘No, I got my business.’ But when property is not safe, when cattle disappear, when honest men call—then a citizen must not think only of himself. If the people want me, I accep.”

Arab began to applaud, but Stubb kicked him.

Baugh shook the candidate’s hand.

“You have made a sacrifice which the cattle interests will not forget.”

“What do we do first?” Louie asked.

“Maintain absolute secrecy.”

“When do I announce?”

“To-morrow.”

The announcement appeared in the Willet *Clarion* beneath a portrait taken twelve years earlier. It described Seigerman as the unanimous choice of the livestock interests and an uncompromising enemy of rustling, disorder, monopoly, extravagance, and secret combinations.

Tolliver read the article and asked which livestock interests were supporting him.

“All of them,” said Seigerman.

Mason made the same inquiry and received the same reply.

Old Ricks merely said, “Well, Louie always did keep good whisky,” and continued whittling.

The announcement forced Baugh to manufacture visible political activity. He sent Arab into the country to organize precincts. Arab traveled by train and stage, visiting saloons, livery barns, and several ranches where he had friends. He returned after nine days with mud on his coat, no money, and an expression of national importance.

“How is the country?” Seigerman asked.

“Rising.”

“For me?”

“Like floodwater. If the election were held to-day, you would carry every precinct except possibly Cedar.”

“What is wrong in Cedar?”

“Religious opposition.”

“I give money to the church.”

“That’s the trouble. You gave five dollars to the Methodists and only three to the Baptists. I can adjust it for twenty dollars.”

Seigerman supplied the money.

Arab also reported that imported votes would be required at the convention. The phrase worried Louie.

“Dot must be legal.”

“Entirely,” Arab assured him. “We don’t import the votes themselves. We import the men containing them.”

“How much?”

“For transportation, meals, lodging, cigars, and the customary educational expenses, fifty dollars now. Another hundred when they arrive.”

Stubb objected that Arab’s organization costs exceeded the campaign treasury.

“You can’t move public sentiment for nothing,” Arab replied. “Public sentiment is heavy.”

Baugh supported him. “The sinews of war must be kept flexible.”

The fifty dollars was furnished and divided privately into three equal shares, with the odd two dollars credited to Baugh’s tuition account.

February passed in conferences. Baugh became general chairman, Stubb the representative of conservative capital, and Arab chief of field operations. Their system had the merit of allowing each man to confirm the others while differing upon every detail.

Baugh would announce that the Prairie Consolidated had pledged three hundred votes.

Stubb would say, “Two hundred.”

Arab would consult his book. “Two hundred and eighty-six, with fourteen doubtful.”

Seigerman always accepted the final figure because it had survived disagreement.

At other times Stubb deliberately threatened withdrawal.

“The cattlemen don’t like Louie’s position on fencing,” he would say.

“What is my position?” Seigerman demanded.

“That’s what they don’t understand.”

“I favor legal fences.”

“Too broad.”

“I oppose illegal ones.”

“Too narrow.”

Baugh would mediate. “State that you favor fences where needed, oppose them where harmful, and reserve the right to act according to law.”

“That is my position,” Louie said with relief.

Arab recorded it as the Seigerman Doctrine.

The candidate’s platform grew. He favored low taxes and sufficient revenue, strict enforcement and individual liberty, better roads without public expense, honest government by practical men, friendship with capital, protection for labor, free grass, open markets, closed jails, and full dinner pails.

On the rustling question he was merciless.

“If elected,” Baugh dictated, “I shall pursue the cattle thief from the branding-pen to the market, from the market to the court, and from the court to the penitentiary.”

“Good,” said Seigerman. “Put in hanging.”

“Too strong for the farmers.”

“Why?”

“Some of them have relatives.”

The political movement also required travel. Baugh went to Junction City to consult a supposed attorney for the Continental. Stubb visited Caldwell to meet the Bar-Circle directors. Arab made a second organization tour. Seigerman paid their railroad fare and furnished expense money.

In Junction City Baugh remained three days, played moderate poker, and returned with a leather portfolio purchased secondhand. It contained cattle circulars, an obsolete railway map, and a blank incorporation form. He carried it thereafter as evidence of responsibility.

Stubb’s mission produced a disagreement of useful proportions.

“The Bar-Circle will not contribute a cent,” he reported in the back room.

Seigerman looked alarmed.

“They promised five hundred dollars,” said Baugh.

“No. They said they might match outside contributions.”

“That is a pledge.”

“That is a maybe wearing boots.”

Arab opened his book. “We don’t need them. Prairie Consolidated will put up eight hundred, the Continental one thousand, and independent stockmen four hundred and sixty.”

“Where is it?” Stubb asked.

“Awaiting a proper time.”

“Money always awaits a proper time when it don’t exist.”

“You represent obstruction,” Arab said.

“And you represent figures that would get lost coming home.”

Baugh quieted them.

“This quarrel must not occur before the candidate. Louie, large corporate contributions made too early would enable our enemies to charge that you are owned by the cattle interests.”

“I am not owned.”

“Of course not. Therefore we shall delay accepting their money.”

Seigerman was satisfied. Indeed, he was relieved. He had already spent more upon the campaign than he admitted to his wife, and the promise of future funds was nearly as agreeable as funds themselves.

He gave Baugh another thirty dollars for postage and confidential telegrams.

By March the three cowboys were living better than at any time since the round-up. Their horses were grain-fed, their clothes repaired, and their personal credit restored. They had even saved a little money, though Baugh forbade gambling.

“You can’t be the political salvation of a county and play faro in public,” he said.

“What about in private?” Arab asked.

“In private you’d still lose.”

They maintained their discipline because spring remained distant and the campaign was generous. At breakfast they discussed precinct totals. At dinner they studied cattle theft. At supper they considered the marshalship.

That prospect had arisen through Arab.

He returned from Topeka with a rumor that the federal marshal might be replaced after the next election. By the time he reached Willet, the rumor had become a plan.

“There is no reason,” he told Seigerman, “why a successful sheriff backed by every major cattle concern should stop at county office.”

Louie’s eyes widened.

“What comes after sheriff?”

“United States marshal.”

Baugh objected at once.

“Premature.”

“I only mention the natural direction of events.”

“National appointments involve senators.”

“I have two senators in correspondence.”

“You have written two senators. That is not the same thing.”

“They will answer when they understand the strength of our organization.”

Stubb shook his head. “Louie hasn’t been nominated for sheriff, and Arab’s already moved him to Washington.”

“A good campaign looks beyond the first water hole.”

Seigerman tried to appear indifferent.

“I do not ask for marshal.”

“Certainly not,” said Arab. “A man who asks never gets it. We arrange the demand.”

“What does a marshal earn?”

Baugh ended the discussion sternly, which convinced Louie that the matter was serious.

From then on the candidate conducted himself with federal dignity. He bought a black broadcloth coat, had new photographs taken, and practiced signing “Louis Seigerman, Sheriff” on hotel stationery. Once, forgetting himself, he added “U.S.M.” beneath it and burned the sheet.

Not every day passed smoothly. There were alarms.

A drover from the Double Spur came into the bar and denied that his company had endorsed Seigerman. Baugh happened to be present.

“Of course they deny it,” he said after the drover left. “Their support is confidential.”

“Why?” Louie asked.

“Because the company has contracts with the present administration. If they declared openly before the convention, those contracts might be endangered.”

Another time the president of the Prairie Consolidated wrote Seigerman in answer to a direct inquiry, saying he had never heard of the political coalition.

“That proves the secrecy of our committee,” Arab explained. “The president isn’t trusted with local details.”

Stubb almost laughed and converted the sound into a cough.

The most dangerous event occurred when Seigerman proposed to visit the Continental and Western ranch and address the riders.

Baugh opposed the trip.

“They are already unanimous.”

“I want to thank them.”

“Gratitude before election looks like weakness.”

“I should meet the superintendent.”

“He is hostile.”

“You say the company supports me.”

“The head office supports you. The superintendent favors Tolliver because Tolliver’s brother married his wife’s cousin. Corporate politics is full of treachery.”

Seigerman abandoned the visit and admired Baugh’s inside knowledge.

As the weather softened, the three campaign managers began watching the southern horizon. Geese passed north. Snow disappeared from the shadowed banks. The streets of Willet changed from iron to mud. Every warm wind carried the smell of wet earth and reminded them that somewhere calves were dropping and outfits would soon be hiring.

Then a letter arrived from the Continental ranch superintendent—not to Baugh, but to Stubb. It said work would begin in two weeks and there would be places for all three if they reported promptly.

Stubb read it in their room.

“The grass has nominated us,” he said.

Arab stretched on the bed. “I was getting tired of politics.”

“You were born tired of everything except counting votes that don’t exist.”

Baugh took the letter and looked thoughtful.

“We must withdraw in order.”

“We can ride out to-morrow,” said Stubb.

“That would be desertion. We are entrusted with a great public movement.”

“We’re entrusted with a room bill.”

“And with the candidate’s confidence. The campaign must be left in a condition able to support itself until it falls.”

Arab grinned. “How much expense money does that require?”

Baugh ignored the question, which meant he was considering it.

They held an emergency meeting with Seigerman that evening. Baugh’s leather portfolio lay open on the table. Stubb looked graver than usual, and Arab had covered three pages of his book with columns.

“We have bad news,” Baugh began.

Louie paled. “The cattlemen withdraw?”

“Never. Their loyalty is firm. The trouble is that our enemies have discovered the extent of your strength.”

“What do they do?”

“They are attempting to stampede the southern delegation.”

Arab struck the table.

“Buying them by the bunch. Tolliver’s men offered five dollars a head in Cedar, whisky in Sand Creek, and two deputyships to a family containing only one voter.”

“Dot is corruption!”

“It is politics,” Stubb said.

Baugh continued.

“We must take the field personally. Stubb must go south and hold the Bar-Circle men. Arab must gather the imported delegation.”

“Legally,” Louie said.

“Always legally,” Arab replied. “Though legality costs more.”

“And you?” Louie asked Baugh.

“I must go to the Continental headquarters. The company’s executive committee has called an urgent conference.”

“How long are you gone?”

“A week. Ten days at most.”

The county convention was three weeks away.

Seigerman looked troubled. He had come to depend upon their conferences. Without Baugh’s authority, Stubb’s objections, and Arab’s figures, the campaign seemed suddenly hollow.

“You come back before convention?”

“Nothing except death or cattle business can prevent us.”

Stubb turned his face away.

“What money is needed?” Louie asked.

Baugh protested. He had not raised the subject. The companies, he said, ought to bear all expenses. Their funds were delayed by accounting regulations and eastern directors who required two signatures to move one dollar. He was unwilling to let Seigerman advance more.

This reluctance was so firm that Seigerman insisted.

After a long argument, Baugh accepted sixty dollars for railroad fare and incidentals. Stubb received forty. Arab required eighty-five because he was moving men, a process comparable in expense to shipping livestock but less certain in delivery.

They planned to leave separately. Arab departed first on the morning train, carrying his organization book and promising to return with four hundred men.

“If I can’t bring four hundred,” he told Seigerman on the platform, “I won’t insult you with less than three hundred.”

Stubb rode south the next day. He shook Louie’s hand in the stable.

“I opposed you at first,” he said, “but you’ve worn down my judgment.”

“I knew you become my friend.”

“I have become something.”

Baugh remained another day. He reviewed the campaign, sealed papers in envelopes, and instructed Seigerman to make no pledges, answer no hostile questions, and distrust any cattleman who denied belonging to the coalition.

“The companies must maintain secrecy until the ballots are cast,” he said.

“When they bring dot money?”

“Convention morning.”

“All of it?”

“Enough to make opposition surrender.”

Louie accompanied him to the edge of town. Baugh rode the black horse and wore the leather portfolio strapped behind his saddle.

“You are sure?” Seigerman asked one last time.

“Louie, if votes were cattle, you could not find range enough to graze your majority.”

They shook hands. Baugh rode south at an easy lope and disappeared beyond a low rise.

That night Seigerman found a letter pushed beneath the door of the back room. It had been written by Baugh, signed also by Stubb and Arab, and addressed to “The Next Sheriff of Comanche County.”

It explained that each man had been called away by urgent cattle business in a different district. Circumstances might prevent their return before the convention, but the organization was complete, the brands were solid, the imported vote was moving, and victory was as certain as sunrise. The letter advised Seigerman to remain calm, avoid unnecessary expenditures, and accept the nomination in a spirit of modest public sacrifice.

Louie read it three times. Its first effect was uneasiness; its second, pride. Important men were always called away upon urgent business. If the organization was complete, their physical presence was unnecessary. Great political machinery, once set in motion, continued by its own weight.

For the next three weeks Seigerman waited.

No campaign funds came from the cattle companies. Baugh had warned him of delays.

No imported voters appeared. Arab had said they would arrive at the last moment to prevent hostile challenges.

No range delegations called upon him. Secrecy, he remembered, was essential.

On convention morning he put on his black coat and walked across to the court-house. The hall was filled with farmers, merchants, town politicians, lawyers, and a scattering of cattlemen. Tolliver’s men wore blue ribbons. Mason’s wore white. Old Ricks had no ribbons, but his friends occupied two rows and smelled confidently of his campaign.

Seigerman looked for the united livestock interests.

He recognized three cowboys. One owed him twelve dollars, one had been barred from his hotel, and the third asked which candidate was giving away cigars.

The convention was called to order. Committees reported, rules were disputed, and speeches were made concerning honest government by men who had already counted every doubtful delegate. Seigerman sat near the front, maintaining the expression Baugh had recommended for overwhelming favorites.

Nominations opened.

Tolliver’s name was presented with loud applause. Mason’s followed. Old Ricks was nominated by a farmer who said the county needed a man familiar with criminals, after which Ricks stood and explained that the speaker meant he had served six years as justice of the peace.

For one alarming minute no one nominated Seigerman.

Then Herman Voelker, a baker and old friend, rose in the back of the hall. He praised Louie’s citizenship, business success, generosity, and excellent table. His speech contained nothing about cattle interests, but it put Seigerman’s name before the convention.

Louie waited for the brands to rise.

None rose.

The first ballot gave Tolliver forty-six votes, Mason thirty-nine, Ricks twenty-seven, and Seigerman one.

Louie stared at the tally. It was a test, he decided. Baugh had often said that powerful organizations concealed their strength on the first ballot.

The second ballot gave him one.

On the third, Tolliver lost two votes to Mason, Ricks gained one, and Seigerman retained his one with a steadiness unmatched by any other candidate.

The fourth produced the same result.

By the fifth ballot people had begun to notice.

A delegate called across the hall, “Louie, your man’s sticking.”

There was laughter. Seigerman turned red but remained seated. The imported delegation might yet arrive. He listened for boots upon the stairs, for the commotion of four hundred lawful residents bearing credentials. He heard only the chairman’s gavel.

On the sixth ballot Mason withdrew. Most of his delegates went to Tolliver, enough to secure the nomination. Seigerman received one vote to the end.

No one ever learned certainly who cast it. Herman Voelker denied doing so, saying he had nominated Louie from friendship but voted for Tolliver from judgment. Seigerman himself swore he had voted for Ricks because Baugh advised a candidate not to appear vain. Several delegates claimed the honor in later years, but only after the ballot had become famous.

That evening the back room at Seigerman’s remained locked.

The three cowboys, meanwhile, were seventy miles south and riding towards the Continental range. They had divided the last expense money, thrown Arab’s organization book into a creek, and resumed their ordinary clothes and language.

At camp the superintendent put them back on the pay-roll. There were calves to brand, fences to mend, and long circles to ride. Corporate rules still forbade feeding unemployed cowboys, but an employed man could eat all the beans he had strength to approach.

For several weeks they said nothing of politics.

Then one evening a hand named Mace returned from Willet. Around the fire he described the convention and Louie’s single vote on six consecutive ballots.

Arab looked offended.

“One vote? I had nine hundred and twelve positively pledged.”

“You must have misplaced nine hundred and eleven,” said Stubb.

Baugh turned a branding iron in the coals.

“The organization failed at the point of delivery.”

“The returns were mighty small,” Mace said.

“Small?” Baugh replied. “They were exact. Louie received the lowest return possible without being entirely excluded. That is not merely small; it is a mathematical distinction.”

Stubb nodded. “Seigerman’s Per Cent.”

The phrase pleased the camp. Within a week it was being used at the chuck-wagon. A horse trader who received one lame mule in settlement for six sound ponies was said to have collected Seigerman’s Per Cent. A cook who baked forty biscuits and found one left for himself got Seigerman’s Per Cent. When a rider courted five girls and secured one dance with the homeliest, the outfit calculated his reward by the same measure.

From the Continental range the expression traveled with round-ups and trail herds. It crossed the Cimarron, went south into the Panhandle, and moved north with beef shipments. Men who had never seen Willet or Louie Seigerman understood it perfectly. It meant the least result that hope, labor, capital, prophecy, and magnificent organization could produce without returning absolute nothing.

As for Louie, he did not run for office again. He continued to keep a good hotel, served generous meals, and required range riders to pay in advance. Whenever cattlemen spoke mysteriously of united interests, he reached under the bar for a club.

Baugh, Stubb, and Arab Ab never revisited his house.

They were not ashamed, exactly. Shame was an emotion for which winter unemployment allowed little room. They maintained that the cattle companies had withdrawn the chuck-line, public ambition had supplied another, and they had merely followed it until green grass returned.

But when any one asked Baugh how close Seigerman had come to becoming sheriff—or United States marshal—he would gaze across the range with the solemn look of a man consulting official returns.

“Within one vote,” he would say, “of receiving none at all.”

# The Keeper of Lost Hours

Every morning at seven, when the bells of Saint Orra struck the hour, Elias Vale opened the narrow blue door beneath the railway bridge and swept yesterday’s time from the floor.

It gathered in the corners like silver dust.

Most people walked past without noticing the door. They hurried toward offices, markets, schools, and factories, carrying umbrellas, briefcases, or half-eaten pieces of toast. Above them, trains shook the iron bridge and sent pigeons flapping into the gray sky. To anyone who happened to glance down, the sign over Elias’s door appeared to read:

**VALE & SON, CLOCK REPAIR**

But there had never been a son, and Elias repaired very few clocks.

Behind the blue door lay a workshop filled with glass jars. Thousands stood on shelves from floor to ceiling, each holding a small quantity of light. Some glowed warm and golden. Some flickered like winter stars. Others were pale as milk.

They were lost hours.

People misplaced time more often than they realized. Five minutes dropped while staring through a rainy window. An afternoon lost to grief. A summer forgotten after childhood. A final conversation delayed until it could never happen. Such hours slipped loose from memory and rolled away, finding their way through cracks in the city until, sooner or later, they appeared as silver dust beneath Elias’s bridge.

His task was to collect them, polish them, and keep them safe.

On each jar he wrote a name, a date, and—if he could discover it—the place where the hour belonged.

**MARA VENN — 14 OCTOBER — THE HOSPITAL GARDEN**

**JONAS PIKE — 3 JUNE — BESIDE THE RIVER**

**UNKNOWN CHILD — MIDSUMMER — A RED KITE**

For thirty-seven years Elias had guarded the lost hours. He had returned some. Many remained unclaimed.

He lived alone in two rooms above the workshop. He ate boiled eggs for breakfast, soup for supper, and one square of dark chocolate before bed. On Sundays he visited the cemetery and sat beside a stone bearing the name of his wife, Clara.

He never spoke to her there. He had said everything he knew how to say before she died.

Or so he told himself.

One November morning, Elias found an entire hour lying in the center of the floor.

Usually lost time arrived in fragments: a few bright grains, a thin thread of light, perhaps a minute beating like a tiny heart. But this was whole. It hovered an inch above the boards, turning slowly, round and luminous. Within it, shadows moved.

Elias shut the door quickly and drew the curtains.

He placed a glass bell over the hour and examined it through a magnifying lens. He saw a long table set for two. Candles. A loaf of bread. A woman in a green dress standing by an open window.

Clara.

Elias dropped the lens.

The hour pulsed beneath the glass.

For several minutes, he could not move. Then he turned away and gripped the edge of his workbench until the room steadied.

It was impossible. The dead did not lose time. Their hours were fixed, sealed by the end of their lives. He had never found a single grain belonging to someone buried.

Yet Clara stood inside that hour exactly as he remembered her at thirty-two: dark hair pinned carelessly, one hand resting on the window frame, a faint line between her eyebrows.

Elias forced himself to look again.

The man seated at the table had his back to him, but Elias recognized his own narrow shoulders. This was their old apartment on Bell Street. The yellow walls. The blue cups. Rain on the window. A white envelope beside the bread.

He knew the date before the label typed itself inside his mind.

The evening Clara left him.

Not the final leaving. That came twenty-one years later, in a hospital room that smelled of soap and lilies.

This was the first.

Elias carried the hour to his strongest cabinet, locked it inside, and put the key in his pocket. Then he swept the floor twice, though there was no dust left to gather.

At ten o’clock, someone knocked.

The sound was so unexpected that Elias stood perfectly still.

People rarely knocked. Those who needed him usually found themselves already inside, confused about how they had entered. The lost were drawn to their time without understanding why.

The knock came again: three sharp taps.

Elias opened the door a hand’s width.

A girl stood outside. She was perhaps fourteen, with brown skin, black curls escaping from a yellow woolen hat, and a schoolbag covered in patches. Rain shone on her coat.

“Are you Mr. Vale?” she asked.

“There is no other Mr. Vale.”

“Do you fix clocks?”

“Occasionally.”

She held up a pocket watch. Its case was brass, scarred and dull.

“It belongs to my grandfather,” she said. “It stopped yesterday.”

“Then take it to Harren’s on King Street.”

“I did. Mr. Harren said there was nothing wrong with it.”

Elias frowned. “A stopped watch has something wrong with it.”

“That’s what I said.”

Against his better judgment, he let her enter.

The girl looked around the workshop, and her eyes widened at the shelves. Most visitors saw only clocks, tools, and boxes. The mind disguised what it was not prepared to understand.

But the girl whispered, “They’re beautiful.”

Elias closed the door.

“What do you see?”

“Jars.”

“What is inside them?”

“Time.”

He took the pocket watch from her.

The hands had stopped at 4:17. When Elias pressed the release, the case sprang open. Instead of gears, he found a small dark hollow that seemed deeper than the watch itself.

“When did your grandfather die?” he asked.

The girl drew a breath. “Yesterday. At 4:17.”

“I’m sorry.”

“He gave me the watch last week. He said I’d know where to take it.”

Elias turned it over. On the back, nearly erased by years of handling, were the initials O.V.

His heart tightened.

“What was your grandfather’s name?”

“Orin Vale.”

The watch slipped from Elias’s fingers and landed on the padded workbench.

The girl watched him carefully. “He said you might do that.”

Elias sat down.

Orin had been his younger brother.

They had not spoken in forty years.

As boys, they had shared everything: a room under the eaves, a red bicycle, a secret language, and the belief that no locked door could remain locked if one had enough patience. Then their father died and left the workshop to Elias. Orin wanted to sell it. Elias refused.

Harsh words became cruel words. Orin left the city. Letters came at first, then stopped. Pride did the quiet work of distance.

Elias stared at the girl.

“You are Orin’s granddaughter?”

“Nina.”

“Why didn’t he come himself?”

“He was sick for a long time.”

“That is not what I meant.”

“I know.” Nina removed her wet hat. “He said you were both stubborn, but you had more practice.”

Despite himself, Elias almost smiled.

Nina pointed toward the pocket watch. “Can you fix it?”

“No.”

“He said you would say that too.”

“Your grandfather seems to have formed many opinions about me.”

“He had forty years.”

Elias picked up the watch again. The dark hollow inside trembled. Something was trapped there, but it was not an hour. It was a path.

“Did Orin tell you what this watch does?”

“He said it goes where regret points.”

“That sounds like him. Dramatic and unhelpful.”

“He also said you’d understand.”

Unfortunately, Elias did.

The watch had belonged to their father. It was the first object Elias had seen hold time. When they were children, he and Orin discovered that if they wound it backward at midnight, it revealed moments people wished to recover.

Their father called it a dangerous toy.

“Regret,” he once told them, “is a compass that always points behind you. Follow it too long and you’ll forget the road ahead.”

After his death, the watch vanished. Elias assumed Orin had taken it.

Now it had returned, empty and stopped at the minute of Orin’s death.

“There should be something inside,” Elias murmured.

“A spring?”

“An hour.”

Nina glanced at the shelves. “His?”

“Perhaps.”

She stepped closer. “Can we find it?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because hours belonging to the dead cannot be found.”

“There are a lot of things people say can’t be found. Mostly they mean they don’t want to look.”

“You sound like him.”

“Good.”

Elias’s hand moved toward the cabinet key in his pocket.

First Clara’s impossible hour. Then Orin’s watch. Two violations of the oldest rule in his life, arriving before noon on the same day.

He disliked coincidences. They were usually patterns wearing masks.

“Come back tomorrow,” he said.

“I’m here now.”

“I have work.”

Nina surveyed the silent room. “It doesn’t look urgent.”

“All time is urgent.”

“Then we should hurry.”

Elias pointed to the door.

She put on her hat but paused before leaving.

“My grandfather’s last word was your name,” she said. “I thought you should know.”

The blue door closed behind her.

For the rest of the day, Elias tried not to think. He cleaned jars, repaired labels, and sorted minutes by date. At sunset he went upstairs, warmed his soup, and did not eat it.

At midnight, he returned to the workshop.

He took Orin’s watch from the bench and Clara’s hour from the cabinet.

The hour glowed more brightly now. Inside it, Clara waited at the window while his younger self sat at the table. That evening had never been lost before. Elias remembered every word.

Clara had received an offer to study music in Vienna for one year. Elias had just inherited the workshop. He could not leave, and she would not stay.

“You care more for other people’s lost time than for ours,” she had told him.

“That isn’t fair.”

“It is exactly fair.”

“If you go, don’t expect me to wait.”

“I’m not asking you to wait. I’m asking you to come.”

He refused.

She left in the rain. One year later she returned. They married and were happy, more often than not, until illness took her.

Elias had always believed the recovered happiness proved he had made the right choice. Yet he also knew Clara had never played the piano professionally again.

He wound the pocket watch backward.

Once.

Twice.

On the third turn, the watch began to tick.

Clara’s hour rose from beneath the glass and stretched into a long ribbon of light. It wound around the workshop, passed through the blue door, and vanished into the night.

Elias grabbed his coat and followed.

Nina was waiting outside.

“I knew you’d do it at midnight,” she said.

“How?”

“My grandfather said that’s when you always did dangerous things.”

Elias had no answer.

The glowing ribbon moved along the pavement. Nina followed it, and Elias followed Nina.

It led them through streets slick with rain, past shuttered shops and empty tram stops. The city changed as they walked. Neon signs became gas lamps. Cars blurred into horse-drawn carriages and back again. Buildings rose, crumbled, and rebuilt themselves in the corners of Elias’s vision.

“Don’t touch anything,” he warned.

“What happens if I do?”

“I don’t know.”

“That means you’ve never tried.”

“It means don’t touch anything.”

The ribbon brought them to Saint Orra Station. The gates were locked, but the pocket watch clicked, and the iron bars opened like folding hands.

Inside, no ordinary trains were running.

A black locomotive waited at the far platform. Its windows shone with the amber light of late afternoon. Above it hung a sign:

**DEPARTED HOURS — NO RETURN TICKET**

Nina climbed aboard before Elias could stop her.

The carriage was filled with passengers who were not truly there. A soldier repeatedly opened a letter. A mother lifted a sleeping baby from a cradle. Two old men played the final move of a chess game. Each scene lasted a few seconds before beginning again.

“These are memories,” Nina said.

“Regrets,” Elias corrected.

“Is there a difference?”

“A memory asks to be carried. A regret asks to be changed.”

They moved through the carriages. With each door, Elias felt the weight of unlived lives pressing around him. Apologies never offered. Voyages never taken. Hands never held.

At the final carriage, they found Orin.

He sat alone beside the window, not as an old man but as he had been at twenty-five: broad-faced, red-haired, impatient. The white scar above his eyebrow came from the day he and Elias crashed their shared bicycle into a stone wall.

Orin looked up.

“You took your time,” he said.

Elias could not breathe.

Nina whispered, “Granddad?”

Orin smiled at her. “Hello, starling.”

She moved toward him, but Elias caught her shoulder.

“He isn’t alive,” he said gently.

“I know.”

Orin’s smile faded. “She knows more than you think.”

“What is this?” Elias asked. “Why is Clara’s hour here?”

“Because it was never Clara’s.”

Orin pointed to the light circling Elias’s wrist.

“It was yours.”

“That hour is not lost. I remember it.”

“You remember what happened. Not what it meant.”

The train began to move.

Outside, the station dissolved into darkness. Scenes appeared in the windows: Elias and Orin as children racing along a canal; Clara at a piano; Orin holding his infant daughter; Nina learning to walk.

Orin leaned back.

“When Father left you the workshop, I thought it meant he loved you more. I wanted to sell it because I couldn’t bear the idea of you becoming him.”

“Our father helped people.”

“Our father hid from them. So did you.”

Elias stiffened.

“You know nothing of my life.”

“I know you missed my wedding.”

“You didn’t invite me.”

“I know you returned every letter I sent after Clara got sick.”

Elias looked away.

“I was angry.”

“So was I.”

The train gathered speed. The scenes outside blurred.

Nina sat opposite her grandfather. “Why did the watch stop?”

“Because I put my last hour inside it,” Orin said. “I meant it for Elias.”

“Hours of the dead cannot be recovered,” Elias said.

“Not from the dead. But I gave mine away while I was still living.”

The darkness beyond the window opened onto a hospital room.

Old Orin lay in bed, thin and pale. Nina sat beside him, gripping the pocket watch. A clock on the wall showed 3:17—one hour before his death.

“He gave you his final hour,” Elias said.

Nina nodded slowly. “He asked me to leave the room. I thought he wanted to sleep.”

“He used the watch to send the hour backward,” said young Orin. “But it caught on your regret, Elias. That evening with Clara was the strongest road leading to you.”

“Why?”

“Because it was the moment you decided staying was always nobler than leaving.”

The words struck harder than accusation.

Elias saw the pattern of his life: the workshop, the bridge, the jars, the cemetery. He had called his stillness loyalty. He had called his fear duty. Even after Clara returned, even after they built a life together, some part of him remained at that table, defending the choice not to follow.

“What did you want me to see?” he asked.

Orin gestured to the hospital scene.

The final hour unfolded.

Elias expected a confession or message. Instead, he watched his brother sleep. Rain tapped the glass. A nurse changed a vase of flowers. Orin woke once and turned toward the empty chair beside him.

That was all.

An hour of waiting.

“You thought I would come,” Elias whispered.

“I hoped.”

“I didn’t know.”

“You knew I was ill.”

Elias lowered his head.

“I’m sorry.”

The train shuddered.

Every passenger in every carriage turned toward him.

An apology to the dead was a dangerous thing. The dead could not accept it, and so the words remained in the world, heavy and unfinished.

But Orin smiled.

“Say it to the living,” he replied.

Cracks of white light spread across the windows.

The train was reaching the end of its track.

“What happens now?” Nina asked.

“The hour returns to the person it was given to,” Orin said.

Elias looked at the pocket watch. “But it was given to me.”

“No,” said Nina.

She understood first.

Orin had not sent his last hour so Elias could keep it. He had sent it so Elias could choose what to do with it.

A whole hour could not restore the dead. It could not change the past. But placed in the hands of the living, it could become sixty unwritten minutes.

A return ticket.

The carriage began to come apart. The chess players vanished. The soldier’s letter scattered into sparks. The sleeping baby’s blanket became light.

Elias grabbed Nina’s hand.

Orin stood by the window, already fading.

“Wait,” Elias said. There were forty years of questions and no time to ask them.

Orin touched the scar above his eyebrow and grinned.

“You were steering the bicycle,” he said.

Then he was gone.

The train disappeared.

Elias and Nina stood in the workshop beneath the railway bridge. Morning sunlight pressed against the curtains. The shelves were quiet.

In Nina’s palm lay the pocket watch.

Its hands showed 3:17.

“Open it,” Elias said.

Inside, the dark hollow had filled with gold.

An untouched hour waited there.

Nina looked at him. “What do we do with it?”

Elias thought of all the ways people tried to use recovered time. They returned to lovers, prevented accidents, changed decisions, and whispered warnings to younger selves. Sometimes they found peace. More often they created new regrets.

Then he remembered Orin’s words.

Say it to the living.

“You keep it,” Elias said.

“For what?”

“For nothing yet.”

He took a blank label from his desk and wrote:

**NINA VALE — ONE HOUR — THE ROAD AHEAD**

He attached it to the watch chain.

Nina read the label twice. “Does this mean I’m your apprentice?”

“It means you possess an hour.”

“The sign says Vale and Son.”

“You are neither.”

“We could repaint it.”

Elias looked around the workshop. For thirty-seven years, he had guarded time as though keeping it safe was the same as using it well. Dust lay thick on the highest shelves. Thousands of hours glimmered in their jars, waiting for people who might never come.

He opened the curtains.

Morning flooded the room.

Under true sunlight, the labels changed. Names Elias had thought permanent faded, and new words appeared. The hours had never belonged only to those who lost them. Some were meant to be given.

**TO SOMEONE WHO NEEDS COURAGE**

**TO SOMEONE WHO HAS FORGOTTEN JOY**

**TO SOMEONE WHO MUST SAY GOODBYE**

Elias began to laugh.

It was a rusty sound, almost a cough. Nina stared, then laughed with him.

Above them, Saint Orra’s bells rang seven.

Elias unlocked the blue door and turned the sign around. For the first time in decades, the lettering showed exactly what was written there:

**VALE & VALE, KEEPERS OF LOST HOURS**

“First lesson,” he said.

Nina removed her coat and hung it beside his.

“About clocks?”

“About sweeping.”

“That’s disappointing.”

“Time often is.”

Together they gathered the silver dust from the corners. Nina worked too quickly and sent bright clouds spinning through the air. Elias began to correct her, then stopped. The workshop filled with glittering minutes, each one catching the sunlight before settling gently into place.

Later that morning, Elias wrote a letter to Orin’s daughter.

After lunch, he visited Clara’s grave. He told her about the train, the watch, and the girl in the yellow hat. He told her she had been right about Vienna. He told her he was sorry.

The dead did not answer.

The autumn wind moved through the cemetery trees, carrying leaves over the stones and down toward the city.

Elias sat quietly until he understood that silence was not the same as emptiness.

Then he stood and walked back beneath the railway bridge, where Nina was waiting with the door open and a newly painted sign above her head.

For once, Elias did not hurry.

For once, he did not remain still.

And the hour ahead of him, bright and unclaimed, began.
